claims.claim: In 1665, the astronomer Cassini saw a dark oval on Jupiter.
claims.source_checked: doi:10.1029/2024GL108993, full text at https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1029/2024GL108993 (fetched via Firecrawl scrape, HTTP 200, citation_doi/volume 51/issue 12 match; not in the Firecrawl research index)
claims.note: Abstract: 'G. D. Cassini discovered in 1665 the presence of a dark oval at the GRS latitude, known as the "Permanent Spot" (PS)'. Sec. 3.1: 'first reported by G. D. Cassini and other astronomers in July-September 1665'. Sec. 3.1 also mentions a possible earlier sighting by Bandtius (1632); that does not contradict 'Cassini saw' in 1665.

claims.claim: Hook as heard by a viewer who swipes at second two: only 'In 1665, the astronomer Cassini saw a dark oval on Jupiter.'
claims.note: The first sentence on its own asserts only that Cassini saw a dark oval in 1665, which is true; it does not say the oval was the Great Red Spot, and the correction comes in the very next sentence. Condition: no on-screen text, title or visual may label Cassini's oval as the Great Red Spot during this first line (A6/E2). Otherwise the popular 'GRS seen since 1665' myth is what the viewer leaves with. Re-check once on-screen strings exist.

claims.claim: It was probably not the Great Red Spot.
claims.note: Abstract: 'PS is unlikely to correspond to the current GRS'. Plain Language Summary: 'most likely the current GRS ... is not the Permanent Spot'. 'Probably not' matches that hedge.

claims.claim: Astronomers kept reporting his spot until 1713.
claims.note: Sec. 3.1: 'PS was subsequently observed by Cassini and others in 1667, 1672, 1677, 1685-1687, 1690-1691, 1694, 1708, and was last reported in 1713 by M. Maraldi'. The reports were intermittent, which 'kept reporting' can carry.

claims.claim: Then, for about a hundred and eighteen years, nobody recorded it at all.
claims.note: Sec. 3.1: 'No reports of PS or any sign of its presence exists in the available observations of Jupiter between 1713 and 1831, a long period of ~118 years'. The paper adds that drawings by Messier (1769), Herschel (1778), Schroeter (1785-86) and others show no such spot. 1831-1713 = 118.

claims.claim: The storm we call the Great Red Spot first shows up in drawings in 1831.
claims.note: Sec. 3.1: 'The first drawings showing the signature of the current GRS, recorded by its Hollow, date back to 1831'. Abstract: 'the current GRS, that was first observed in 1831'. The 1831 sign is the Hollow, not yet a red oval (reddish only ~1872-1876); 'shows up' is fine, but visuals should not draw a red spot for 1831 (A6).

claims.claim: And Cassini's spot was only a third to a half as long as the Great Red Spot was in 1879.
claims.note: Sec. 3.2: 'The length of PS is 2-3 times smaller than that of the 1879 GRS.' 'Length' is the zonal (east-west) length, so 'as long as' is the right dimension. 2-3 times smaller = 1/3 to 1/2.

claims.claim: To be the same storm, it would have had to keep growing for more than a century, unseen.
claims.note: Sec. 3.2: 'PS would have had to grow steadily from 1713 to 1879 at a rate of ~+0.14 deg/year (160 km/year) to be the GRS. This is highly unlikely since ... no reports of PS or GRS exist during this long period'. Growth spans 166 years, and the unseen part alone (1713-1831) is 118 years, so 'more than a century, unseen' holds either way.

claims.claim: No storm on Jupiter has ever been seen to grow like that.
claims.note: Sec. 3.2: 'no continuously sustained grow in size has been never reported in Jupiter's vortices'. 'Like that' (steady, century-long growth) keeps it true; the GRS itself grew transiently in ~1927-1939 (Sec. 3.2), which is not sustained growth. 'Storm' for 'vortex' is a normal simplification.

claims.claim: So the Great Red Spot is nearly two hundred years old.
claims.note: The source gives a lower bound, not an age: 'The current GRS has therefore certainly been in existence for 193 years' (counted from the first 1831 drawing). It gives no formation date, and its simulations describe a faint, elongated proto-GRS. 'Is nearly two hundred years old' states the age as about 195, which goes beyond the source (A3). Change to 'So the Great Red Spot has been on record for nearly two hundred years.' or 'So the Great Red Spot is at least nearly two hundred years old.' The figure itself is fine: 2026-1831 = 195.

claims.claim: Cassini's spot was most likely a different storm, long gone.
claims.note: Sec. 3.1: 'it is most likely that this lack of observations during such a large period means that PS disappeared.' Abstract: 'PS is unlikely to correspond to the current GRS'. Sec. 3.2 also refers to 'the GRS disappearance (as was the case of PS)'.
